Is this really a race issue? The article seems to try really hard to paint it as one but it seems more like an income issue to me. She isn't making enough money to afford a lot of the properties in her "ideal neighborhood", so she has to settle for a poorer neighborhood. It happens to be the case that poorer neighborhoods tend to be black, but there's a very chicken-egg kind of relationship here:

Poor communities tend to have higher rates of crime, delinquency and poorer public education. This leads to adults that drop out of school, resort to crime, or graduate but don't get very well-paying jobs. For the top cut of the group that manage to make a success of themselves in the face of adversity, a better paying job and saving up means moving out of a poor community and into a wealthier one.

I've read several studies indicating that this pattern has nothing to do with race, and yet we find that these poor communities are dominantly black and latino. Are we simply seeing the long-term effects of systematic racism failing to work its way out due to poor social mobility or is there some deeper systemic racism actually taking place? I personally feel that the former is more likely than the latter, and government regulation hamstringing growth in the middle class is largely to blame.

Community and education reform may help as well, but poor inner-city communities tend not to have the funding for such programs in the first place.
